title: Converting, Parsing, and Validating Values
learningObjectives: Distinguish conversion, parsing, and validation as related but different operations.
Explain why input values often begin as text regardless of intended meaning.
Identify safe conversion steps and handle conversion failures.
Validate a converted value against rules and acceptable ranges.
Avoid treating conversion success as proof that a value is correct or trustworthy.

understand.concept: Conversion changes a value from one representation or type to another. Parsing interprets text according to a format or grammar to produce a meaningful value. Validation checks whether the resulting value satisfies rules such as required fields, allowed ranges, or domain constraints. These steps may occur together but serve different purposes.
understand.whyItMatters: Programs frequently receive text from forms, files, APIs, or sensors. A value may be syntactically convertible yet still be invalid for the task—for example, a parsed age of -3 or an order quantity of zero.
understand.analogy: Parsing is reading a form and understanding what each field says. Conversion is putting the understood value into a usable format. Validation is checking whether the form meets the rules before accepting it.
understand.analogyLimit: Validation depends on context and business rules. A value valid in one system may be invalid in another. Parsing and conversion libraries may accept surprising formats unless configured carefully.

explain.narrative: Treat external input as untrusted. First interpret the input using an expected format, then convert it to the intended representation, and finally validate its meaning and constraints. Handle errors explicitly instead of silently substituting defaults. For example, '12abc' should not be accepted as a valid quantity merely because a permissive parser extracts 12. Also validate ranges, required fields, relationships, and normalization rules where appropriate.

examples.title: Parse text as an integer
examples.explanation: Parsing produces a number from the text. The radix is specified to avoid ambiguity.

examples.title: Reject text that is not a complete numeric value
examples.explanation: A strict numeric conversion yields an invalid numeric result instead of accepting the trailing letters; check the conversion outcome.

examples.title: Validate a range after conversion
examples.code: const age = 17; const valid = Number.isInteger(age) && age >= 0 && age <= 120;
examples.explanation: The value is numeric but validation also checks the allowed domain.

examples.title: Check an empty field separately
examples.explanation: An empty string may convert to zero in some APIs, so requiredness should be checked independently.

examples.title: Handle a conversion failure
examples.code: const raw = 'abc'; const parsed = Number(raw); if (!Number.isFinite(parsed)) { /* report error */ }
examples.explanation: Conversion outcome is checked so invalid input is not used as if it were a number.

commonMistakes: Accepting partial numeric strings without checking the entire input.
Assuming conversion automatically checks allowed ranges or domain rules.
Treating empty input as a legitimate zero without explicit policy.
Silently replacing invalid data with a default and hiding the failure.
